newsitem.title: UK: Bullish stock markets face October jitters.
newsitem.headline: Bullish stock markets face October jitters.

text.p: Major world bourses may have raced to record highs lately but some superstitious investors still fear the October jinx and the approach of Saturday's anniversary of the 1987 market crash.
Wall Street, where an ageing bull market is showing few signs of fatigue, reached another milestone during the past week when the Dow closed above 6,000 for the first time ever.
The remarkable advance in the U.S. hoisted stock markets in Britain and Germany into unchartered territory, and helped power France's CAC-40 index to its highest level since May 1994.

While professional investors have so far ignored the October factor this year, memories of "Black Monday" aren't far below the surface. The month has spooked investors ever since the 1929 Wall Street crash, which took place in October.

Robert Hitt, publisher of AstroEcon, a U.S.-based astrological stock forecasting service, warned that world stock markets are poised to collapse within the next six months, as Uranus, Saturn and Pluto move into a configuration similar to that of 1929.

"These three planets are traditionally the most difficult for individuals to deal with and the mass psychology presented by this pattern serves to get the maximum number of people in financial trouble," said Hitt.
"The most dangerous times are mid-November of this year and the February-April period next year, he said.
This astrological pattern represents a "mid-point" cycle that takes place only once every 66 years or so, he added.
But another non-economic theory says it will be years before the stock market crashes again.

"There's a theory that you won't see more than one stock market crash in your lifetime because if you lived through one, you're always wary," said Joseph Reynoso, managing director of Apollo Derivatives.
"Once that wary generation passes, the investment public gets filled with hubris and when that happens, there's the possibility of it happening again...I don't know if I believe it," he added.
Market strategists say that the global stock market rally can continue as long as the "dream combination" of steady growth and low inflation lasts.
The biggest and most immediate risk to world stock markets comes from the U.S., where any hint of economic strength could reignite concerns about inflation and higher interest rates.
"The risk is still that if we get one bad (economic) number out of the U.S., that could reverse everything," said Gary Dugan, European strategist at U.S. investment bank J.P. Morgan.
Some market watchers predict U.S. stocks will retreat after the predidential election in November, which incumbent Bill Clinton looks set to win comfortably.

Historically, there have been no losses in the stock market in the months of October or December when incumbent parties retained the White House, noted Yale Hirsch, publisher of the Stock Traders Almanac.

Bull markets tend to occur in the third and fourth years of presidential terms while markets tend to decline in the first and second years. And most of the big bear markets began after elections, Hirsch noted.

U.S. stock strategist Elaine Garzarelli, who made her name predicting the 1987 meltdown, is one bull who turned bearish several months ago and is now forecasting a 15 to 25 percent correction in the U.S. equity market.

Yet even as Wall Street embarks upon the seventh year of its bull market, the longest on record, the bear camp is becoming i ncreasingly vacant. Conventional wisdom says a bull market turns sour when it it sucks in the last of the bears.

Even long-time bear Byron Wien, Morgan Stanley's chief U.S. equity strategist, earlier this month raised his equity exposure, reversing a previously bearish position. Wein's change of heart didn't go unnoticed on Wall Street, but investors continued to chase U.S. share prices higher.
But UK equity strategist Scott Evan of UBS said he does not believe investors are euphoric.

"A significant correction in the U.S. would definitely hurt European markets, but the UK market is on solid ground," said Evan. "A number of factors could have knocked in lower recently if it wasn't well supported."

Evan noted that UK shares shrugged off the UK government's changes to the taxation on share buybacks and special dividends a few weeks ago. More recently, the market rose despite disappointing reports on domestic inflation, and has pushed higher even though the large corporate acquisitions that many had been expecting have failed to materialize, he said.
But as fund manager George Soros once warned, "The usual bull market successfully weathers a number of tests until it is considered invulnerable, whereupon it is ripe for a bust."
